case_studies.title: Pairing Matters: Performance, Failures, and Efficiency in Lightweight Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: Self-hosting coding agents is often necessary for software-engineering teams that must keep proprietary code and development traces within controlled infrastructure. Lightweight, open-weight models make such deployment more feasible by reducing hardware requirements, while strong results on repository-level benchmarks demonstrate their potential for demanding coding tasks. Deploying these models as coding agents requires pairing them with an agent harness, making their joint performance a key deployment consideration. Yet existing leaderboards primarily report fixed harness-model configuration
case_studies.summary: The study shows that pairing lightweight open‑weight coding models with the right agent harness can give strong performance on coding tasks while keeping hardware costs low. The researchers tested different harness‑model combinations and found that the choice of harness significantly affects speed, failure rates and overall efficiency. The result is a set of guidelines for choosing a harness that matches a given model to optimise performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown:
If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do:
1. Identify the lightweight model you plan to host.
2. Test the model with several harness options to benchmark speed and failure rates.
3. Choose the harness that gives the best performance‑to‑cost ratio and allocate resources accordingly.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper focuses on lightweight coding agents suitable for self-hosted environments, directly relevant to IT engineering teams managing proprietary code. The concepts are mature enough to be implemented in existing workflows, and the approach could be turned into a commercial SaaS or internal tool within a few months.

case_studies.title: Reimagining Enterprise RAG for Multi-Agent Systems: A Knowledge Layer That Organizes Before It Retrieves
case_studies.abstract: Enterprises are deploying agentic AI across the software development lifecycle, and they need the behavioral logic of the systems they act on, not stakeholder documentation. A seven-agent reverse-engineering pipeline recovered this logic, processing 241 repositories across 18 services into thousands of artifacts describing scope, journeys, rules and acceptance criteria. Recovery does not confer usability. Entities like offer, eligibility, and activation recur across services under a shared vocabulary, related in name but operationally distinct, so one end-to-end journey implicates over a thous
case_studies.summary: The study shows how a seven‑agent pipeline can reverse‑engineer business logic from 241 code repositories, turning raw code into thousands of structured artifacts like scopes, journeys and rules. It demonstrated that similar concepts (e.g., offer, eligibility, activation) can be mapped to a shared vocabulary across services. For cloud infrastructure managers, this research is not directly relevant to day‑to‑day operations.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a reverse-engineering pipeline for agentic AI, which could influence software engineering workflows. However, it remains largely theoretical with no released code or deployed system. The applicability to IT infrastructure is limited and monetisation is uncertain within 90 days.

case_studies.title: ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retr
case_studies.summary: ActionRAG addresses memory errors in large‑language‑model agents by combining careful indexing with a graph‑based retrieval that can revise similarity scores on the fly, reducing entity fragmentation and improving evidence consistency. The authors built a graph‑diffusion memory architecture that flags and corrects indexing mistakes and refines search results during queries, showing better recall and precision in long‑term memory tests. For IT infrastructure managers this research is not directly relevant to cloud management or operations.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.relevance_tag: AI memory architecture for LLM agents
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a graph-based memory system for LLM agents, which could potentially benefit internal automation and knowledge management for IT engineers. However, it appears to be a research prototype with no released code or proven deployment. The direct applicability and commercial readiness within 90 days are limited. Thus the overall scores are low.
